standard.title: Money values and representation
standard.description: recognise the relationships between dollars and cents and represent money values in different ways
standard.prior_knowledge: No direct predecessor identified in the progression map at Y3. Students have used money in additive modelling contexts at Y2 (AC9M2N06) but have not yet formally studied the dollar-cent relationship or represented money values in multiple ways.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students recognise the relationship between dollars and cents and represent money amounts in different equivalent forms.

nodes.label: Dollar and cent relationship
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can state that 100 cents = $1 and use this to convert between dollar and cent representations.
nodes.minimum_width: Convert three money amounts between cents and dollars; explain the relationship (100 cents = $1).
nodes.typical_width: Convert money amounts between cents and dollars in both directions; explain the place value connection — dollars are units, cents are hundredths.
wider: Investigate how different countries use different currencies and coin systems, comparing structures
Connect the dollar-cent relationship to the decimal place value system — setting up understanding of decimal notation for money amounts

response_modes.reason: The 100-based relationship between dollars and cents requires explicit connection to place value — students who understand this as a conversion rule without place value grounding often make errors in mixed notation (e.g. writing $1.50 as $1.5 or $150).

nodes.hinge_reason: The dollar-cent conversion with place value grounding is required for Node 2 and for AC9M3N06 financial modelling tasks — students who have only a mechanical rule (not a place value understanding) produce systematic errors in mixed notation and in making-change calculations.
success_criteria: Students can convert a cents amount to dollars and cents (e.g. 375¢ = $3.75).
Students can convert a dollar amount to cents (e.g. $4.20 = 420¢).

nodes.label: Representing money values in different ways
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can represent a given money amount using different combinations of coins and notes, and identify equivalent representations.
nodes.minimum_width: Represent one money amount using two different combinations of coins and notes; confirm both are equivalent.
nodes.typical_width: Represent money amounts using multiple coin and note combinations; find the most efficient representation; connect to making change.
wider: Explore cashless payment contexts — how digital transactions represent money without physical coins, and what stays the same
Investigate how First Nations Australian communities have engaged with exchange and value systems, and how these compare to the dollar-cent system

response_modes.reason: Students often have only one mental model of a money amount (e.g. always thinking of it as a sum of the smallest coins). Seeing equivalent representations across varied combinations builds flexibility and prepares for making change.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The cashless payment and cultural comparison contexts extend money understanding beyond physical coins into representation and value systems more broadly — genuinely enriching for the concept without acceleration.
success_criteria: Students can show two different ways to represent the same money amount using coins and notes.
Students can identify which combination of coins/notes is more efficient for a given amount.
